source_text: At si esset in natura crimen, Petri erat imperita sententia, qui censuerat videlicet ad immaculatae sanctitatis testimonium posse sufficere, si actus eius a criminibus vindicaret; cum crederetur in eo habitare peccatum per naturale virus. Igitur si de naturali malo aliquid ille sensisset, sollicitius partem hanc commemorasset et pressius, ut scriberet, Christus nobis reliquit exemplum, qui peccatum nec fecit, nec quod nos trahimus nascendo, collegit; sicque merito sequeretur, inventum in ore eius dolum non esse. Porro si hoc putasset, numquam commemorationem fecisset exempli; quem enim hominibus esse ostenderet imitandum, si illum externae carnis natura discrevisset, et censuram magisterii substantiae diversitas arguisset?
pass_a_gloss: But if there were a charge in nature, Peter's sentence was unskilled, who had judged namely that it could suffice for a testimony of unspotted holiness if his act vindicated him from charges; when sin was believed to dwell in him through a natural virus. Therefore if he had sensed something about natural evil, he would have commemorated this part more anxiously and more pressingly, so that he would write, Christ left us an example, who neither did sin, nor gathered what we draw by being born; and thus it would deservedly follow that deceit was not found in his mouth. Further if he had thought this, he would never have made commemoration of an example; for whom would he show to humans as to be imitated, if the nature of an external flesh had distinguished him, and a diversity of substance had accused the censure of the teaching?

pass_b_english: But if there were a crime in nature, Peter’s statement would have been ignorant. He evidently judged it sufficient testimony to spotless holiness to clear Christ’s actions of crimes, although sin would be believed to dwell in him through natural poison. If Peter had thought anything of natural evil, he would therefore have mentioned this part more carefully and emphatically. He would have written, “Christ left us an example: he neither committed sin nor acquired the sin we inherit at birth.” Then it could fittingly follow that no deceit was found in his mouth (compare 1 Peter 2:21–22). But if Peter had thought this, he would never have mentioned an example. For whom would he have presented for human beings to imitate if the nature of an alien flesh had set Christ apart, and a difference of substance had impeached the authority of his teaching?

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
